agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Optimising High-Entropy Alloys for Hydrogen Storage Solutions for South Africa and Sudan’s Energy Sectors
descriptions:
==Background==
The quest for a sustainable future necessitates reducing carbon and water footprints to meet 2050 decarbonization targets. With the rising energy demand due to population growth, transitioning from fossil fuels to cleaner alternatives is crucial. Hydrogen, notable for its high energy density and environmentally friendly combustion by-product (water), is a key player in this transition. However, challenges persist regarding the safety and cost of hydrogen storage infrastructure, particularly with high-pressure and low-temperature requirements. Current storage methods fall short of the United States Department of Energy's targets, highlighting the need for advanced solutions. Metal hydrides, such as Mg, Al, and Ti, offer promising avenues but face cyclability, activation conditions, and kinetics limitations.
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have recently emerged as potential candidates for hydrogen storage, especially those with a body-centred cubic (BCC) structure with superior storage properties. However, the mechanisms behind their high storage capacities remain unclear. This project aims to develop novel TiVZrNbCrX-based HEAs with exceptional hydrogen storage capabilities by exploring compositional variations and processing routes. The research will leverage computational methods to predict critical parameters and experimental validation to identify optimal alloys.

==Aim==
The primary aim of this project is to develop novel high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with exceptional hydrogen storage capabilities. This involves tuning the composition and phase constituents of TiVZrNbCrX-based HEAs to achieve faster charge-discharge kinetics, improved reversibility, minimal storage capacity decay, and efficient hydrogen absorption and desorption at ambient conditions. The project will explore a wide compositional space by incorporating elements such as Mn, Fe, Mo, and Mg in various ratios, guided by computational predictions. Additionally, the influence of processing routes on the hydrogen storage properties of the HEAs will be investigated to establish the mechanisms driving enhanced performance.

==Technical Objectives:==
1.Using computational methods, Predict critical parameters for enhanced hydrogen storage properties in TiVNbCrX-based HEAs.
2.Assess the influence of processing routes and composition on the phase constituents of selected alloys.
3.Evaluate the hydrogen storage properties of the selected alloys, focusing on composition, processing routes, and phase constituents.
4.Identify the underlying mechanisms influencing hydrogen storage properties and determine the alloy with the best combination of properties.

==Social Objectives:=
1.Establish strong collaborations between researchers in the UK, South Africa, and Sudan to share sustainable resources and build capacity.
2.Foster relationships with government, industry, and policy stakeholders through symposiums and webinars to accelerate the hydrogen economy in the Southern African region.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Development of long-acting nanosuspensions for chemoprophylaxis of malaria
descriptions: threatening hundreds of millions of people. With nearly 250 million infections yearly, the malaria burden is enormously disproportioned for the African Region. The United Nations and the World Health Organization are urging the research community to develop new strategies for the management of malaria. While vaccines are only available for falciparum malaria in children, vivax malaria is considered a neglected disease. Causal and suppressive chemoprevention of malaria is indicated to people travelling to endemic areas. However, these regimes are inconvenient, requiring medication up to 1 week pre- and 4 weeks post-travelling to endemic areas, with users often missing doses or stopping treatment due to pill fatigue and gastrointestinal side effects. Crucially, erratic bioavailability and typical fluctuations in drug plasma concentration of conventional oral treatments lead to development of parasite resistance. In this scenario, long-acting drug delivery can play a significant role in preventing malaria. Leveraging on the approval of long-acting injectable nanosuspensions (LAI-NSs) for HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis, this proposal aims to develop LAI-NSs of antimalarial agents able to produce sustained therapeutic plasma concentrations and protect users for at least 3 months after a single injection. LAI-NSs are suspensions of solid nanocrystalline particles made of the pure drug (nanocrystals), which can form intramuscular depots and lead to sustained drug release. An international team will combine unique areas of expertise to achieve the project’s aims, i.e., drug formulation (Queen’s University Belfast, UK), experimental malaria models (Fiocruz Institute, Brazil), and public health and epidemiology (Manhiça Health Research Centre, Mozambique). The proposed workplan involves the development of LAI-NSs and full characterisation in vitro and in vivo, including pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies, which will be carried out between the UK and Brazilian partners. Translational activities will be led by the Mozambique team and will include focus groups and in-depth interviews with healthcare personnel, and meetings with regulatory bodies in all three countries. The overall aim of this project is to develop a solution to malaria which, in the longer term, will directly improve the welfare, and result in economic benefits for the two partner low- and middle-income countries. The outcomes of this project could revolutionise the management of malaria, increasing user adherence, reducing risk of developing parasite resistance, enhancing efficacy, and reducing the burden for healthcare systems. This Award will help to establish an international network that will lead research in malaria, nurturing talent with a comprehensive plan of training activities.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: A collaboration to establish a paediatric research and outreach center in northeast Brazil for health promotion in marginalized groups
descriptions: The World Health Organisation, UNICEF, and the Lancet emphasised prioritising children in the Sustainable Development Goals. While governments are crucial, universities and educators also have significant roles in achieving these aims. Therefore, a partnership between the Children's Health Exercise Research Centre and the Federal University of Rio Grande do Norte (UFRN), aims to enhance research capacity and to start a children's health research centre in Natal, Brazil. The partnership includes a cross-sectional investigation into vascular dysfunction, a key aspect of atherosclerosis that starts in childhood. Evidence from high-income regions shows that movement behaviour (physical activity, sedentary time, and sleep) and fitness are vital for vascular function in children, but these often decline during adolescence, especially in girls. There is a research gap in understanding vascular function in the transition to adolescence in low and middle-income areas. This study aims to understand how movement behaviour, along with physical fitness, impact vascular physiology in boys and girls transitioning to adolescence. To address this, 1200 children aged 9-14 will be randomly selected from schools in Natal be evaluated. Children will undergo fasted blood sampling for cardiovascular risk factors, resting vascular function/structure assessment (arterial stiffness, intima-media thickness, and flow-mediated dilation), body composition and anthropometry measurements, a cardiorespiratory fitness assessment, and a post-exercise vascular health assessment. Participants will also complete socioeconomic and behaviour questionnaires. At the end of data collection accelerometers will be provided to record movement behaviours. Analysis will involve general linear models with mediation/interaction analysis. Upon completion, each participant will receive an illustrated, age-appropriate book detailing their health status, with tips for improving vascular health. This study will be the first in the global south to investigate vascular physiology in boys and girls and the mechanisms linked with movement behaviours and fitness. Additionally, the project includes outreach initiatives to engage participants, families, and schools: 1- Data collection visits: children will visit the university to learn about their health; 2 - Open days: Schoolchildren will be invited to the university to discuss higher education opportunities and children's health; and 3 - Health information weeks: schools will participate in health information weeks when the research team will present findings and provide educational materials on cardiovascular health. These initiatives aim to bridge the gap between scientific knowledge and community involvement, promoting opportunities for children to engage in science and health research through university access.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Investigation of Fouling in Brazil’s Pipeline Systems for Improved Water Supply and Energy Efficiency
descriptions:
An extremely serious issue for the transport of fluids through pipes is fouling, i.e. the formation of unwanted material on the surface of conduits, in most cases due to the deposition of salts. In Brazil, fouling detrimentally affects the distribution of drinking water, the public sanitation system, especially in rural areas, and the transmission of diseases, such as COVID-19. Biofouling is particularly severe in power stations. One paramount example is the Fontes Nova Power Plant, one of the oldest hydroelectric complexes in Brazil, where biofilm often hampers the performances of heat exchangers.

The nature of pipe flow, i.e. laminar, transitional or turbulent, strongly affects the pressure gradient and thus the energy consumption. It is therefore crucial to determine under which conditions the flow transitions from laminar to turbulent to predict the required pressure difference, with and without fouling. Current transition models, however, are of limited use to engineers because the pipeline inlet, where the external disturbances enter the flow and cause the turbulent motion downstream, is often ignored.

Therefore, we want to investigate the effect of fouling on pipe flows, taking into account the entrainment of realistic ambient disturbances at the pipe mouth and the fully-developed turbulent regime. Our research objectives are first to gain a full understanding of the transitional and turbulent flows, with and without fouling, to calculate and measure accurately the increase of pressure gradient due to fouling. We will also obtain correlations, graphically represented by an “extended Moody diagram”, for the pressure gradient along the conduit from the pipe entrance, as a function of the system parameters and fouling characteristics. Our proposed methodology is a powerful blend of theoretical, numerical and experimental methodologies, only made possible by the synergy between Sheffield and Rio. The nonlinear receptivity calculations based on the theoretical/numerical framework developed in Sheffield will be combined with direct numerical simulations of the Navier-Stokes equations. These theoretical/numerical results will be compared with the experimental data obtained in the unique pipe-flow rig in Rio, where the fouling is created by the deposition of particulates. Thanks to our extended Moody diagram, Brazilian engineers will be able (i) to predict the minimum amount of fouling to be removed to achieve a desired flow rate with existing pumps and (ii) to design new pipelines with optimal diameter to accommodate for the fouling growth, thus extending the operational life of these infrastructures, limiting repair, maintenance and replacement costs.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: PANORAMIC: Physicochemical and mechanical studies of agricultural waste-based materials in South Africa and Zambia for sustainable packaging
descriptions:
The proposed PANORAMIC project aims to address the environmental and socio-economic challenges associated with agricultural waste biomass in South Africa, Zambia as well as the broader Southern African region. With approximately 87% of the region's general waste being biodegradable, primarily from agricultural sources, this project focuses on valorizing this biomass to develop biodegradable polymeric composites for sustainable packaging. This initiative aligns with the bio-economy strategies of South Africa and Zambia, emphasizing bio-based industries and renewable products to meet sustainable development goals, including industry innovation and responsible consumption. This project targets various agricultural wastes, including maize stalks, cassava peels, rice husks and non-edible parts of plants like invasive weeds. These materials will undergo physical processing, such as wet and dry milling, to produce stable base materials, which will be enhanced with plasticizers, starch, and glycerol. Characterising the chemical composition, microstructures, and physicochemical and mechanical properties of these materials is essential to guide their development into biopolymer-based composites.

The primary objective of PANORAMIC is to develop sustainable agricultural biomass-based materials suitable for food packaging. To achieve this, the project methodology is structured into three work packages (WPs). WP1 focuses on material selection and chemical composition analysis. A thorough literature review will be conducted, and suitable agricultural waste materials will be identified and analyzed for their chemical compositions. WP2 involves the physicochemical and mechanical characterization of starch samples, formulation, and initial fabrication of biocomposites. This includes detailed characterization of properties such as amylose content, swelling power, solubility patterns, structural morphology, pasting properties, and thermal properties. Initial biocomposite formulations will undergo mechanical testing to assess stiffness and strength. WP3 focuses on optimising biocomposite formulations and developing biodegradable packaging solutions, ensuring product quality and performance through comprehensive testing and confirming environmental sustainability through soil decomposition evaluations.

PANORAMIC will be led by a multidisciplinary research team, to spearhead the biocomposite research and facilitate knowledge transfer through academic exchanges, workshops, and training sessions. By addressing environmental hazards such as methane emissions from landfills and integrating farmers in rural areas like venda into the global economy, PANORAMIC aims to mitigate environmental degradation and improve livelihoods. The project seeks to advance biocomposite research, contribute to sustainable material development, and promote the bio-economy. Through the development of innovative, sustainable packaging solutions, PANORAMIC will position itself as a catalyst for sustainable development in South Africa and Zambia, supporting responsible consumption and production while enhancing the the socio-economic well-being of agricultural communities.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Naphthoquinoidal Compounds for Bioimaging and Innovations Against Neglected Diseases in Brazil and Sierra Leone (NUBIAN)
descriptions: Over 8 million people in Latin America suffer from Chagas disease, with up to 70 million at risk of chronic infection, highlighting the urgent need for effective treatments. This disease, caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, receives minimal attention from Western pharmaceutical companies. Similarly, Human African Trypanosomiasis (HAT), or sleeping sickness, is a major public health issue in sub-Saharan Africa, caused by Trypanosoma brucei and transmitted by tsetse flies. HAT affects about 60 million people and causes up to 50,000 deaths annually across 36 African countries. Both diseases are neglected tropical diseases requiring innovative therapeutic solutions. This proposal addresses the UN Sustainable Development Goal 3 (Good Health and Well-Being) by focusing on an experimental-theoretical approach to develop sustainable methods for creating a library of naphthoquinoidal compounds with potential antiprotozoal applications. Based on our extensive experience in developing and characterising quinone-based bioactive compounds, we aim to utilise click chemistry to synthesise a novel class of 1,4-naphthoquinone-based sulfur(VI) fluoride exchange (SuFEx) hybrids. This approach combines the potent trypanocidal activity of naphthoquinones with the introduction of sulfur-containing groups, privileged motifs found in various pharmacologically effective substances and natural products. SuFEx represents the latest set of ideal click chemistry transformations, with S(VI)–F motifs successfully used as connective linkers in polymer synthesis and the construction of various functional molecules. The theoretical component is crucial for understanding reaction mechanisms, predicting experimentally viable SuFEx derivatives through high-throughput screening, and describing their fluorescent properties, the latter of relevance because we predict that some of the compounds will exhibit fluorescence properties that make them relevant for bioimaging. Computational studies will provide insights into the electronic structures and reactivity patterns of the synthesised compounds, guiding experimental efforts and contributing to a database of potential SuFEx-functionalised targets. Additionally, the project will establish the Sierra Leone UK Centre for Advanced Studies on Tropical and Infectious Diseases (SLUK-CASTRID) to investigate naphthoquinoidal compounds in the context of sleeping sickness. It will serve as a model for capacity building in other developing countries, driving scientific innovation and addressing local health challenges. This initiative's impact will extend beyond the current project, laying the foundation for future research and the development of new therapeutic agents for various neglected tropical diseases. Overall, this project will significantly advance the development of new therapeutic agents for Chagas disease and HAT, while also fostering sustainable development and improving health outcomes on a global scale.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Transforming Agriculture Residues to Bio-Composite Solutions for Sustainable Growth and Energy Efficiency in Brazil and Bangladesh (TERRA)
descriptions:
Brazil and Bangladesh, despite their geographical and cultural differences, share significant challenges related to energy consumption, climate change, and sustainable development. Brazil struggles with inefficient electricity usage in buildings, while Bangladesh lacks universal electrification and clean cooking solutions. Electricity demand is continuously increasing due to population growth, living standards (air conditioning/clean cooking) upgradation and rising demand for cooling. In Brazil, electricity is the biggest source of energy in buildings. Residential buildings account for 28.2% of the electricity consumption in Brazil (electric water heater represents 19% of residential electricity consumption) and air conditioning consumption is increasing in the last years. Conversely, in Bangladesh, there is no universal electrification, and clean cooking remains a critical issue, with rural households (65% of the population) predominantly relying on traditional biomass fuels, leading to significant indoor air pollution and health problems. Both countries hold significant potential for solar technologies to tackle their energy challenges. Brazil underutilizes its vast solar resources, while Bangladesh is making progress with solar mini-grids/off-grid systems to electrify remote areas. Moreover, both countries face another challenge: managing a substantial amount of agricultural waste. 
Recent research demonstrates the potential to use agricultural residues to prepare composite phase change materials (PCMs) for energy applications such as carbon (ash) to enhance thermal conductivity, rice husk and sugarcane bagasse for shape-stabilized PCMs, and sugarcane bagasse wax, but this is still in the development stage. The composite PCMs could be used to store excess of thermal energy, such as solar energy during peak sunlight hours and use this energy for other applications like hot water, passive cooling or clean cooking, particularly beneficial in off-grid or unreliable-grid situations or to regulate the temperature in a system to improve the performance such as PV or building materials. 
This research focuses on transforming and integrating agricultural waste into Shape-Stabilized Phase Change Materials (SSPCMs) for energy-efficient applications (PV, building). This innovative project tackles energy challenges in Brazil and Bangladesh by harnessing a readily available resource: agricultural waste. We aim to transform first and second-generation byproducts into high-value SSPCMs and integrate them into a range of energy-efficient applications such as PV panels, and building systems in Brazil and to improve the efficiency of energy systems for cooking in Bangladesh. This research is particularly relevant considering the growing energy demands in both countries, the global emphasis on sustainability, and the increasing concern over waste management.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Aggregation-induced delayed fluorescence in Pesticide and Herbicide Detection (APHiD) for the Brazilian Agricultural Industry
descriptions:
Brazil is one of the biggest consumers of pesticides in the world and preventing them, herbicides and other toxic elements from permeating through the food chain is of great importance. To effectively reduce this contamination of food pathways, early and accurate detection of pesticides and herbicides is necessary. Here we plan to utilise aggregation-induced emission (AIE) and aggregation-induced delayed fluorescence (AIDF) as markers for the presence of pesticides and herbicides. The ultimate aim is to develop a prototype solid-state sensor utilising AIE and AIDF molecules that has the potential to be used in the field.  AIE molecules have become well-established in sensing applications, and a lot of the best-performing materials are commercially available. There are even initial reports of their use as pesticide and herbicide sensors. This work aims to elaborate and expand their utilisation in this field and introduce AIDF materials that have the additional parameter of lifetime changes (alongside all the original benefits of AIE) to help reduce the chance of false positives and provide an extra level of analysis and scrutiny. It is very timely to introduce AIDF into pesticide and herbicide sensing as there is recent significant development in portable lifetime measurement techniques. This project, entitled APHiD, will use AIE and AIDF to develop new methods for testing pesticides and herbicides based on fluorescence intensity, colour and lifetime. The three main objectives are:

1) Benchmark existing AIE compounds in terms of morphology and fluorescence response to pesticides and herbicides. 

2) Extend this benchmarking to commercial AIDF compounds to capture the additional lifetime response.

3) Design and develop solid-state sensors based on AIE and AIDF compounds for use in the field and laboratory.

Development in this area of pesticide and herbicide detection will have a great impact on the Brazilian economy and will strengthen food security for the local populace and their international exports. This project will bring together an international team of core knowledge and expertise to tackle this problem. More importantly, part of that international team (led by Dr Leonardo Furini) will also have the necessary local expertise and network to ensure any outputs and deliverables will have a direct pathway to the stakeholders.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Sustainable dressings for complex wounds: Blue Amazon actives in 3D-printed biomaterials for wound healing
descriptions:
Treating complex wounds, such as the ones derived from burns and infections, with the aim of wound closure and tissue regeneration, is still a significant healthcare challenge worldwide. Exploring natural bioactives and biomaterials has been fundamental in developing new dressings that can help tackle this problem. Marine products, in particular, have been the focus of some Brazilian companies, with the government supporting the industry-healthcare complex development, particularly in the production of active ingredients (both through synthesis and extraction). As emphasised during the recent pandemic, a strong healthcare industry is critical for the economic development of any country, and Brazil still suffers from having to import certain classes of medicines, such as those used to treat severe burns.
The use of microalgae as a source of active compounds is still relatively recent, but many unique molecules with anti-inflammatory, analgesic and wound healing properties have been described in the last two decades, including C-phycocyanin (C-PC). In this project, we aim to optimise the purification of C-PC to pharmaceutical grade and load it in new 3D printed wound dressings to treat damaged tissue. For this purpose, we will use chromatographic and filtration purification methods and load C-PC into lipid-based nanocarriers, which will later be incorporated into polymeric filaments for 3D printing, leading to drug-loaded wound dressings. Our approach will include scalable and transferable techniques, facilitating the development of prototypes for pre-clinical and clinical testing. Given the versatility of 3D printing techniques, these dressings will be able to be manufactured on small scales in remote sites or at larger scales in industry. We aim to obtain at least one optimised prototype that promotes the healing of skin cells and reduces the inflammatory response triggered by pathological microorganisms or their components.
Besides the detailed scientific objectives, this project aims to establish a long-lasting collaboration between two early career scientists in the UK and Brazil. Also, it will reinforce the research capacity of the Federal University of Bahia (UFBA) and De Montfort University (DMU) through knowledge exchange and skills development. Thus, this proposal supports the development of new wound healing products while reinforcing the Brazilian academic research environment, its industry-healthcare system and the overall workforce in pharmaceutical development and manufacturing.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: UK-SA Collaboration to Combat Drug-Resistant Infections: Advancing Novel Metal-Based Antimicrobials for South Africa and Other Low- to Middle-Income C
descriptions:
The emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a severe threat to global health, disproportionately affecting low- to middle-income countries (LMICs) such as South Africa, where AMR-related deaths are significant. The decline in novel antibiotic development has necessitated alternative approaches to address this crisis. Transition metal complexes, particularly metal carbonyl compounds, have shown promise as potential antimicrobials. Preliminary data suggest these compounds possess favorable antibacterial properties and low toxicity, warranting further exploration.
This project aims to promote economic development and improve welfare in developing countries, specifically targeting South Africa, through the development of innovative antimicrobial solutions. The primary goals include:
1. Synthesis and Characterization of Novel Ligands:
 We will design and synthesize a diverse array of P,N-Schiff base ligands and novel N,X,N-based ligands. These will be fully characterised for their physicochemical properties. A total of 60 novel ligands will be prepared within the scope of this project.
2. Synthesis and Characterization of Metal Carbonyl Complexes:
 We will synthesize, characterize, and structurally elucidate new rhenium, manganese, molybdenum, and tungsten carbonyl complexes using the prepared ligands. For these syntheses the prepared ligands and learned expertise will be exchanged between the UK and South African labs to foster collaboration and innovation. We aim to prepare at least 20 novel metal carbonyl complexes for each of the of the four metals.
3. Evaluation of Photophysical Properties:
We will Investigate the photoluminescence properties of the novel metal carbonyl complexes to further characterize them with the goal to identify candidates suitable for fluorescence imaging in bacteria.
4. Biological Assessment:
 We will conduct comprehensive biological evaluations to assess the antibacterial activity of the synthesized complexes. This will be supplemented by toxicity and stability studies of promising compounds to identify lead candidates for further development. Initial mechanism of action studies will elucidate putative target sites for these new compounds in bacteria
This collaborative research between the UK and South Africa aims to address the urgent need for new antibiotics, contributing to the economic development and welfare of South Africa by tackling a critical public health issue. The project will also enhance scientific capacity and foster international collaboration, ultimately benefiting LMICs through improved healthcare outcomes and reduced AMR-related mortality.
By focusing on the synthesis and evaluation of novel metal carbonyl compounds, this research has the potential to yield new, effective antimicrobial agents, significantly impacting the fight against AMR in developing countries and around the globe.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Small-scale vertical-axis wind turbines for backup domestic electricity generation in rural South African communities
descriptions:
The proposed project combines the experimental aerodynamics expertise at Queen Mary University of London and the University of the Witwatersrand to develop a low-cost vertical-axis wind turbine that can be installed in a single household and can generate sufficient energy for lighting and phone charging. The project addresses the impact of unreliable power generation on disadvantaged socioeconomic communities in South Africa. The lack of electricity during power outages contributes to interruption of economic output, an unsafe environment, and disruption to education, which disproportionately affects those from poorer communities and women. Due to their low cost and high electricity-producing potential per footprint area, vertical-axis wind turbines show considerable promise in addressing this problem. However, devices currently on the market have a large diameter (in excess of 2 metres), which is too large a footprint for a domestic household and also exceeds the purchasing power of most rural households. In addition, the power generated by such devices is typically surplus to the requirements of emergency devices, such as mobile phone chargers, so there is a clear need to develop a smaller-scale turbine which is cheap and small enough for domestic settings in South Africa but nevertheless provides sufficient power to satisfy back-up power requirements.

There has been very limited research on vertical-axis wind turbines at the lower Reynolds numbers (10,000) associated with small-scale devices and so the proposed project seeks to develop a vertical-axis wind turbine through a series of wind tunnel experiments which optimise key design parameters (such as solidity and blade profile) and provide physical insight into self-starting characteristics, the ingestion of flow by the turbine and the interference between blades. To ensure safe operation of the turbine in close proximity to people, it is essential to avoid blade failure due to fatigue loading and so further wind tunnel tests will quantify the structural loading on the blades throughout their motion cycle. Finally, in order to transfer the findings from wind tunnel experiments to real-life settings in rural South Africa, representative environmental tests will be carried out using a highly-instrumented prototype of the optimised turbine to establish the aerodynamic performance and blade loading during real-life operation. By developing a small-scale, vertical-axis turbine and characterising its performance, the project will constitute considerable progress towards the development of a device that can contribute to reducing socioeconomic inequality in South Africa by mitigating the effects of power outages in rural, domestic settings.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Extremes in Brazilian Amazon lakes and its implications for social-ecological systems
descriptions: The Amazon Basin, encompassing one of the world's most significant river systems, plays a critical role in global biodiversity and sustains the livelihoods of millions of people. However, the region faces increasing threats from extreme climate events, such as extreme temperatures, floods, and droughts, which pose severe risks to its socio-economic stability. This project aims to address these challenges by exploring the occurrence, impacts, and underlying mechanisms of extreme and compound events in Amazonian waters, with a specific focus on enhancing the resilience of local communities. The primary beneficiaries of this research will be the Amazonian communities, who are disproportionately affected by these climatic extremes. The project is designed to be fully compliant with the Official Development Assistance (ODA) criteria, ensuring that its primary purpose is to promote the economic development and welfare of these communities, which are comparable to some of the world's least developed regions in terms of human development indices. Indeed, these communities are closer to LDC development levels compared to other regions of Brazil, and the project directly targets their economic development and welfare. For instance, human development indices in the Tefé’s region municipalities range from 0.49 to 0.6418, comparable to some Sub-Saharan African Nations (e.g., 0.516 in Sudan). Our approach integrates historical data analysis, remote sensing, fieldwork, and predictive modelling to provide a holistic understanding of extreme events and their impacts on both local and regional scales. Key objectives include engaging with local communities to co-identify challenges, characterizing the frequency and occurrence of extreme events using historical climate data and satellite imagery, assessing the socio-economic impacts on local populations, investigating the compounding effects on aquatic ecosystems, and developing models to forecast future occurrences under various climate scenarios. This will culminate in actionable insights and recommendations for ecosystem management and policy-making. The project is structured into five work packages: project management, sociological impacts of extremes, local-scale model development and validation, large-scale assessment of compound events, and future projections of extremes. Active community engagement will be a cornerstone of this research, involving participatory mapping, semi-structured interviews, and workshops to co-create solutions. Collaborating with the Mamirauá Institute, which has a long history of working with riparian communities, we aim to enhance the resilience of the Amazon Basin by identifying vulnerable areas and populations, proposing targeted conservation efforts, and informing policy decisions. Ultimately, this project will contribute significantly to sustainable ecosystem management and the economic stability of Amazonian communities,

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Data Driven Redesign for Urban Climate Adaptation in Brazilian Informal Settlements
descriptions: The rising urban population in the global South has led to the rapid expansion of informal settlements. In São Paulo, Brazil's largest city with over 11 million people, a large part of the residents live in such settlements. Informal settlements are often characterised by lack of formal urban planning, inadequate access to basic infrastructure and poor housing conditions. Informal houses are typically self-constructed with inadequate methods and materials, resulting in poor thermal performance, increased risks of thermal stress for the occupants and overreliance to unsafe energy sources. As the climate crisis continues to exacerbate the incidents of extreme heat in the region, reducing the vulnerability of the population by decreasing these risks is critical. This research proposal aims to develop a data-driven approach to build capacity and resilience in the marginalised community of São Remo. Working closely with the local community to co-create and co-design adaptation strategies for energy efficiency improvements in the housing stock which are practical and acceptable to the community. By making use of open access data and tools, the developed methods will strengthen the capacity of the local population on decision making, contributing to long-term sustainability and resilience. The implementation of participatory processes throughout the project will ensure collaboration through peer-to-peer learning networks, increasing public awareness and enhancing impact. The findings will serve as a model of redesigning informal settlements for urban climate adaptation for similar urban contexts across São Paulo, informing policymakers, practitioners and local residents about effective strategies for intervention and promoting sustainable and inclusive development in this rapidly urbanising city.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Next Generation Assays To Unpick The Spectrum Of Tuberculosis in Madagascar and South Africa
descriptions:
Background:
Tuberculosis (TB) remains a leading infectious cause of death globally, with the vast majority of the disease burden in less developed countries. Increasing understanding of the natural history of TB suggests a spectrum of infection and disease, including subclinical states. However, existing tests such as interferon-gamma release-assays (IGRAs) do not discriminate these states. M. tuberculosis-specific T cell activation shows promise to detect recent infection, while blood RNA biomarkers may detect early disease. In this project, we will develop and evaluate these immunological and molecular assays to unravel the spectrum of TB.
Objectives:
1.To evaluate a T cell antigen-specific activation (TB-TASA) assay for subclinical TB in a South African cohort.
2.To test the generalisability of the TB-TASA assay among people with TB infection and clinical disease in UK cohorts.
3.To test the generalisability of the TB-TASA assay among people with TB infection and clinical disease in Madagascar.
4.To use multimodal data to discriminate the spectrum of TB across settings.
Methods:
1.We will use biobanked samples from a cohort of household TB contacts in South Africa. In a nested case-control design, we will perform the TB-TASA assay among people with clinical (n=50) and subclinical (n=60) TB, and healthy IGRA-positive people (n=50). 
2.We will use biobanked samples from people with clinical disease (n=40) and healthy, IGRA-positive individuals (n=40) from London TB services, to evaluate the sensitivity and specificity of the TB-TASA assay in a low incidence setting. 
3.We will prospectively sample from TB patients (n=15), their household contacts (n=30), and community controls (n=30) in Madagascar, to evaluate the TB-TASA assay in a least developed setting when using fresh, whole blood samples. 
4.We will use paired TB-TASA and blood RNA data from all three countries to evaluate whether multimodal data improves discrimination of infection and disease states, using multivariable statistical and machine learning modelling.
Impact:
TB is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in South Africa and Madagascar, and hampers economic development due to the associated loss of life-years, productivity, healthcare expenditure and catastrophic costs to families. Our analyses will pave the way for better discrimination and understanding of TB states and natural history, while building capacity and collaboration in TB research in the UK, South Africa and Madagascar. Our analyses will include innovation in immunology and data science and will support future multidisciplinary research collaboration across settings with varying TB burden.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Sustainable Road Construction to Aid Mobility and Inclusive Rural Economies in Developing Nations
descriptions:
Rural development is crucial for achieving global sustainability goals, as 80% of those in poverty live in rural areas. Technological and infrastructural advancements, particularly surfaced roads, significantly enhance access to services and economic opportunities, driving economic transformation in rural communities.  In South Africa (SA), nearly one-third of the population resides rurally, with about 26% living more than 2 km from all-season roads. Road construction in SA heavily relies on non-renewable resources such as  gravel, crushed rock, and bitumen. Some of the main challenges faced in developing and maintaining rural roads include funding shortfalls and material availability.  Meanwhile, developed countries are increasingly adopting circular economy strategies using recycled waste materials in road construction to reduce overall costs, minimise environmental impact, and create social value for stakeholders. In this regard, the utilisation of digitisation tools have proven to be essential for overcoming various market barriers to scaling up the circular economy. 
In SA, the circularity of construction materials is only 2%, but studies have shown that adopting circular economy strategies in transportation can significantly reduce environmental impact, create jobs, and stimulate economic growth. However, gaps remain in understanding material availability, digitising circularity functions, and lifecycle costs. There is an urgent need to develop technology and circular material strategies that enable rural populations to access new material value chains for road construction, while simultaneously advancing rural development across multiple spheres.This project aims to develop a regionally implementable road material technology tailored for rural applications, enhancing accessibility and economic growth using regionally available wastes as circular road construction materials.
The methodology followed in the study will initiate and develop a holistic and optimised technological framework encompassing resource mapping and geospatial database development, material-specific processing and economic opportunity creation, tailored engineering application through characterisation and implementation, integration into the circular economy, and lifecycle sustainability assessment. A key deliverable of the project is the development of an open-source platform i.e the digital material information system. This platform will enable stakeholders and practitioners to track and predict the circularity and lifecycle impacts of waste-sourced road materials, ensuring long term transparency and equitable resource management. Additionally, the development of pre-normative guidelines and specifications will set the stage for future standardisation and widespread adoption. The project is envisioned to serve as a model for developing similar rural infrastructure systems in other developing countries, facilitating technology transfer and the dissemination of best practices.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Thermographic Reconstruction and Inversion for Wind Turbine Blades to Advance Renewable Energy in Brazil
descriptions: Brazil, with its commitment to achieving net-zero carbon emissions by 2050, recognizes the pivotal role of wind energy in this transition. The country, boasting an installed wind energy capacity of over 24 GW, is among the top global wind energy producers and aims to reach over 30 GW by 2030. This expansion is essential for maintaining environmental sustainability and protecting Brazil's vast rainforests, which serve as crucial carbon sinks. The development of wind energy infrastructure not only helps reduce carbon emissions but also addresses critical economic, energy, and social challenges, attracting significant investments and fostering economic development. This project focuses on thermography reconstruction and inversion for wind turbine blades (WTBs), leveraging the complementary expertise of UK and Brazilian research teams. Thermography is a critical non-destructive evaluation (NDE) method for inspecting and maintaining WTBs, involving the heating of materials and monitoring surface temperature variations to detect subsurface anomalies. Traditional thermographic methods face significant challenges with WTBs due to their complex geometries, non-uniform heat distribution, and the need for robust forward heat transfer models. To address these challenges, the project aims to develop new-generation thermography reconstruction and inversion methods, specifically designing new induction coils and flash excitation schemes to handle the complex geometries of WTBs, and utilizing physics-based time inversion techniques to create detailed CT-like profiles of blade structures. By collaborating with Brazilian WTB manufacturers such as Aeris to evaluate and validate these methods, the project aims to enhance the sustainability of Brazil's wind energy sector, contribute to global efforts towards net-zero emissions, and address critical environmental challenges. Through this collaborative effort, the project seeks to advance the field of NDE and wind turbine maintenance, increase energy production, and promote sustainable practices and community involvement in Brazil's renewable energy initiatives.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Algae4Africa: Microalgae-based livestock wastewater treatment (MbLWT) in Tanzania
descriptions:
The Algae4Africa project aims to treat livestock wastewater in Tanzania using algae to improve water access and sanitation in rural communities.
Clean water provision is still a major challenge in Tanzania, where it is estimated that about a quarter of the 65 million strong population still do not have access to basic drinking water and sanitation services. As Africa’s second largest cattle producer, agriculture forms a major part of Tanzania’s economy. However, the wastewater discharge from livestock is a potent risk for pollution and groundwater contamination, further compounding the water constraints currently faced by the nation.
The use of algae photobioreactors is an exciting natural solution to this problem, with the growing algae metabolising the residual nutrients and pollutants, while the solar exposure assists the reduction of the pathogen loading. Thin liquid film algae photobioreactors are particularly promising, as their high surface area to volume ratio results in improved gas exchange for algae growth and lowered pumping costs, as less agitation is needed to promote gas exchange. The resulting algae biomass can provide different value streams, such as biofertilizer or textile pigments, to help fund the wastewater treatment.
The project will start by identifying the user needs of the key stakeholders in the Tanzanian livestock keeping communities to ensure the project is fully compatible with the local conditions and communities. 
Livestock wastewater will be collected and analysed in Tanzania to determine nutrient loading, solid loadings and other relevant parameters, which will then be used to develop artificial medium compositions for laboratory work in the partner countries. 
Algae species that can grow in the non-sterile wastewater as well as have high pigment concentrations will then be screened. A thin liquid film photobioreactor will be adapted and built for the local conditions and the performance will be characterised in terms of algae growth rates, drinking water production rates and composition of the treated wastewater. Recovered pigments will be tested for dyeing of pretreated cotton to evaluate colour fastness and other key properties, to optimise the process of pigment extraction, purification and application.
The algae value streams will be investigated to determine the suitability of the algae produced as a biofertiliser through nutrient and elemental analysis, and small-scale growth studies. 
Lastly, the overall system developed within this project will be analysed and evaluated for suitability, both from a social point of view through stakeholder engagement, as well as a techno-economic point of view.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Electrochemical Fluorination to combat Trypanosoma cruzi: Synthesis of Fluorine-Functionalized Naphthoquinoidal Compounds as Treatments for Chagas Dis
descriptions: Over 8 million people suffer from Chagas disease in Latin America and up to 70 million are at risk of chronic infection, therefore finding effective treatments for the disease is an urgent requirement. Unfortunately, like so many tropical diseases, attention from western pharmaceutical companies is very minimal. Quinones are class of compound that have shown exceptional bioactivity against trypanosoma cruzi, the parasite that spreads the disease. However, the cytotoxicity of the compounds that have so far been isolated is too high. New synthetic methods are therefore required to be able to synthesise new quinone derivatives for biological testing. In the project, we will develop new, sustainable ways to make libraries of fluorinated quinones. Fluorine has very beneficial effects on pharmaceutical agents and is incorporated into up to 30% of blockbluster drugs, yet methods to make fluorinated quinones are extremely limited. Key to our strategy is the use of electrochemistry and hypervalent iodine to enhance the sustainability and selectivity of the fluorination reactions. We have identified several related strategies to develop that will lead to large libraries of novel fluorinated quinones, which we anticipate will give high biological activity against trypanosoma cruzi.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Establishing a biobank of blood samples from people living with HTLV-1 to assess druggable metabolic determinants of adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma
descriptions:
"The human T-lymphotropic virus (HTLV-1) is a retrovirus that infects at least 5 to 10 million people worldwide, of which nearly 1 million are estimated to live in Brazil. HTLV-1 infection is characterised by chronic lifelong persistence and a subgroup (approximately 10%) of infected individuals develop disease manifestations. These include adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma (ATLL) which is characterised by limited treatment options and a median survival time of 11 months. Despite the impact of HTLV-1 infection on morbidity and mortality in Brazil, studies on potential markers of disease progression and of therapeutic interventions have been hampered by the low availability of high-quality samples from local patient cohorts, especially from people with ATLL. 
We aim to fill this gap by leveraging our dual expertise on clinical sampling and translational research on retroviruses and HTLV-1. We will establish a biobank of blood and plasma samples obtained from a Brazilian cohort of people living with HTLV-1. Blood samples will be then used to isolate the cell types more susceptible to HTLV-1 infection, i.e., peripheral blood mononuclear cells and CD4 T-lymphocytes. Samples will be subjected to an in-depth investigation of metabolic dysregulation, which is known to be associated with both retroviral infection and tumour transformation. Ongoing research in our UK site indicates that ATLL cells are characterised by a hyper-energetic state, with increased expression of the oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) complexes and of key metabolites sustaining the OXPHOS pathway (NADH) or the detoxification of its metabolic by-products (NADPH). We will assess the physiological relevance of these findings by evaluating the metabolic dysregulation induced by HTLV 1 infection (and ATLL in particular) using samples from our Brazilian cohort. To this aim we will combine large-scale metabolomics in plasma and cells with functional metabolic assays in whole cells as well as in key subcellular compartments (i.e., mitochondria). Samples obtained from local healthy donors, as well as our ongoing work with ATLL cellular models and in vitro infected primary cells, will be used to refine the identification of bona fide markers of disease progression in our patient cohort. These putative markers will be further validated for their single-cell level co-expression with HTLV-1 DNA and for their potential to serve as therapeutic targets in vitro and ex vivo. 
Overall, our study is expected to establish a novel biobank allowing the investigation of markers of HTLV-1 disease progression and of potential strategies to treat it."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Engineering monoclonal antibodies that broadly neutralise snake venom neurotoxins and cytotoxins
descriptions:
Snakebite envenoming results in approximately 130,000 deaths and 400,000 cases of disability every year. Antivenom, the only effective snakebite treatment, is manufactured using a century old approach of collecting plasma from immunised animals. Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) offer a promising alternative approach to current snakebite envenoming therapies and could be used to either supplement or replace existing antivenoms. However, venom is composed of many distinct proteins and isoforms, representing many potential mAbs targets, and only a few specific toxin isoforms contribute to severe snakebite envenoming outcomes such as death and disability. Therefore, it is essential to understand which toxins need to be neutralised to prevent these severe outcomes, as well as which toxin epitopes are conserved for broad neutralisation across multiple isoforms. Three-finger toxins (3FTxs) are the predominant toxins present in Elapidae (cobra, krait, and mamba) venoms and are responsible for lethal neurotoxicity and tissue-damaging cytotoxicity from these species. Here, we aim to identify those 3FTxs that are pathologically relevant to snakebite envenoming, screen isolated mAbs for neutralisation of these key toxins, and engineer mAbs with increased neutralisation breadth and potency using structure-guided design. Rationally improved mAbs and mAb mixtures will be evaluated for neutralising capability using in vitro cell assays for neurotoxicity and cytotoxicity. Additionally, these mAbs and mAb mixtures will be evaluated using preclinical in vivo murine models of snakebite envenoming, matching the guidelines set by the World Health Organisation for the production of antivenoms. These engineered mAbs and mAb mixtures will be the foundation of next generation highly targeted antivenom therapeutics for elapid snakebite envenoming.

The impact of reproducible, safe, broadly effective, and inexpensive next generation antivenom will likely be specific to each country but will undoubtedly have a positive influence on the development of Africa as a whole. Millions of Africans risk being bitten by snakes every year, and without timely access to treatment face death, disability, and further disadvantage. Snakebite most severely affects impoverished or rural communities, and often kills or maims those young and healthy individuals that are community and family providers. As snakebite victims usually cannot identify the snake that bit them, we propose to develop broadly cross- reactive antivenom specific for toxin classes rather than the snake species responsible for envenoming. We are focusing on the three-finger toxins, as these toxins are primarily responsible for death and disability from common and widespread Elapidae (cobra, mamba and krait) snake species. This proposal is of relevance to all African countries where elapid snakes reside. These next generation therapeutics will be more affordable, and independent of the cold-chain requirements that make current antivenom inaccessible to local healthcare providers. By improving public health for low-income or rural households in Africa, this proposal will ultimately contribute towards increased prosperity, security, and wellbeing throughout the continent.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Engineering high-entropy manganese oxide nanocrystals for low-cost, robust rechargeable zinc-air batteries (RZAB)
descriptions:
"The primary challenge of access to clean and affordable energy in Ethiopia and South Africa will be addressed via the development of high-performance, low-cost rechargeable zinc-air batteries (RZAB) based on defect-engineered manganese-based air electrodes, which can be integrated with solar panels for off-grid power generation. Ethiopia and South Africa generate most of their energy from coal and traditional biomass fuels, with their national access to electricity rates standing at 48.6% and 95%%, respectively. Sudden extended rolling blackouts due to load shedding, massive increases in fuel prices and living costs mean fewer people have access to electricity. 

RZAB, also known as a zinc-air fuel cell, is a device capable of reversible conversion of chemical energy to electrical energy. RZAB provides a localized energy source for powering electronic devices, electric vehicles and power reserves while improving access, safety, and reliability. Although RZABs are environmentally friendly, safe, and low-cost, they are limited by weak kinetics of oxygen electrochemistry reactions and the formation of zinc dendrites, among others; all of which lead to poor utilization of zinc, limited energy, and poor cycling efficiency.

Central to creation of RZAB is the development of materials that are readily available, affordable, and sustainable. Manganese accounts for 61% of electrode materials in two popular rechargeable batteries: Lithium-ion-manganese-oxide and Nickel-manganese-cobalt oxide used today. Proof of principle shows that manganese-based air electrodes have the potential to address these key challenges of RZAB while being low-cost, safe, and environmentally friendly with high energy density in comparison to cobalt used in popular batteries today.

Accordingly, we propose an interdisciplinary collaborative research partnership for the development of high-performance, low-cost RZAB. We will develop defect-engineered electrodes that are compatible with RZAB which can be used as a standalone or coupled device i.e., solar panels to enable infrastructure to run smoothly irrespective of time, season, and energy disruptions.  Electrodes will use low-cost and readily available minerals such as manganese and zinc, to which Ethiopia and South Africa have access to abundant reserves in Debarwa, En-Kafala, Northern Cape and Limpopo, respectively. In this way, our international partnership seeks to apply locally sourced materials from Ethiopia and South Africa to solve a problem affecting a substantial number of the most disadvantaged sectors while simultaneously improving equitable energy access and reliability which is a catalyst for developing economic activity, health, and lifestyle improvement (UN SDG 3: Good Health and Well-Being, 7: Affordable and Clean Energy, 13: Climate Action)."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Machine Learning-driven Optimisation of Hybrid Steel-Concrete System for Offshore Wind Turbine Towers
descriptions:
"According to Brazil’s 2050 National Energy Plan, the federal energy research office has set targets to install 16GW of offshore wind power capacity by 2050. The absence of operational offshore wind projects to date is due to a lack of advanced offshore wind turbine technology and local supply chains. The next generation of offshore wind turbines, with capacities reaching 15-20 megawatts and rotor diameters over 250 meters, requires higher and stronger towers. The conventional steel tubular tower design demands thicker steel sections (more than 80 mm as opposed to 40-60 mm for onshore) for offshore applications owing to the shell buckling-dominated design. This thickness has exceeded current Brazil's steel manufacturing capabilities. To meet its 2050 targets, Brazil needs to develop a cost-effective, low-maintenance solution for high-performance turbine towers well-suited to its environmental conditions and local resources. 
The project aims to assist Brazil in achieving its 2050 offshore wind energy targets by developing a design optimisation framework of a cost-effective offshore wind turbine tower system. A hybrid steel-concrete structural system using concrete-filled double-skin steel tubular (CFDST) sections is examined in the project. CFDST sections have been shown to offer excellent structural efficiency and constructability over conventional steel tubular sections in a range of heavy structural applications, such as columns in high-rise buildings, and piers in bridges. The improved structural efficiency is attributed principally to composite action between the steel tube and the concrete infill, in particular, the reduced susceptibility to local buckling of the tubes owing to the presence of the concrete infill, as well as the increased strength and ductility of the concrete infill due to the confinement offered by the steel tubes. More importantly, CFDST sections use thinner steel tubes readily available in Brazil and improve the cost-effectiveness of offshore towers through savings in material, foundation and labour costs. 

However, optimally designing CFDST systems has been an extremely challenging task due to highly nonlinear and complex component interactions, and there are no existing design guidelines available for CFDST sections applied to large-scale wind turbine towers. Machine Learning (ML) techniques offer a promising alternative for handling complex problems and have been recently applied by the UoN team to characterise the behaviour of complex structural systems. Therefore, this project will address the design optimisation of CFDST systems through testing, numerical modelling, along with various ML techniques, aiming to offer economic and sustainable tower design solutions for offshore wind turbines in Brazil."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Internation Collaboration Advancing the Craft of Platinum Jewellery Through 3D Printing for South African Makers, Designers, Academics, and Industry
descriptions: South Africa is rich in platinum group metals (PGMs), producing 70%-80% of the world’s primary produced platinum. However, the country often exports these materials in their raw form, missing out on the value-added processes. A 3D printing jewellery industry can offer more opportunities for local ownership and benefit-sharing, creating value-added products from raw materials to exports and addressing some of the economic inequalities that exist in South African. However, there is a strong need to enhance the suitability of platinum alloys for 3D printing in the jewellery industry. This research aims to address the challenges via developing modified platinum alloys that can offer the jewellery industry new opportunities in terms of design, efficiency, and cost-effectiveness. This will be done to harness the power of data-driven materials development techniques, coupled with experimental validation, to develop platinum alloys optimised for 3D printing of jewelleries. By building an international collaboration on 3D printing technology for platinum, offering skill training and workshops, South Africa could foster innovation and value-added manufacturing on 3D printing of jewelleries, creating jobs in the manufacturing sectors.

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Interlocking prefabricated 3D-printed low-carbon concrete wall panels for low-income housing construction in South Africa
descriptions:
"South Africa's built environment is segregated into ‘formal’ and ‘informal’ sectors, with the latter comprising government-subsidised low-income housing (LIH) units in the poor urban periphery. The LIH units, exclusively built for very low-income households, are 40 m2 low-cost, single-storey, stand-alone dwellings built with unreinforced conventional masonry units, namely concrete blocks and burnt clay bricks. The following challenges are associated with LIH units: 

(1) A growing backlog of over 2.6 million LIH units exists, meaning over 15 million vulnerable South Africans are in dire need of LIH units. 

(2) The LIH units have very poor construction quality, which not only causes significant detriment for LIH residents but also imposes a tremendous cost of rectification to the government. 

(3) The thermal performance of conventional masonry walls of LIH units is poor, contributing to residents’ discomfort.

(4) The use of concrete and burnt clay in large volumes has a significant negative environmental impact. The production of cement, an ingredient of concrete, is highly energy- and carbon-intensive. With the new carbon tax in South Africa, cement manufacturers will be penalised for their carbon emissions, causing concrete masonry unit prices to increase.

Another challenge in South Africa is that approximately 85% of the nation’s electricity is generated via coal-fired power stations, which produce about 40 million tons of fly ash annually, of which 36 million tons of fly ash are disposed of in fly ash ponds and landfills annually creating significant environmental risks. Fly ash disposal occupies lands which can potentially be used for other purposes.

This project aims to tackle the above challenges by developing an “interlocking prefabricated 3D-printed low-carbon concrete wall panel” system for LIH construction. The proposed system is expected to: 

(a) significantly enhance the construction quality and reduce the construction time of LIH units. This is because panels will (i) be prefabricated using 3D-concrete-printing technology in a factory setting, (ii) be lightweight, and (iii) have an interlocking mechanism so they can be easily and quickly connected together and installed on-site; 

(b) significantly enhance the sustainability of LIH units, because panels will be made of low-carbon geopolymer concrete using South African fly ash. Carbon emissions from geopolymer production are up to 80% less than cement;

(c) significantly enhance the thermal and fire performances of LIH units, enhancing the residents' comfort and safety;

(d) be a cost-competitive solution where the production and installation cost of panels will be comparable to conventional methods."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Low-cost sustainable nanomaterial-based water purification systems with rapid on-site detection of pathogens at resource-limited settings.
descriptions:
"The provision of accessible and affordable clean water is one of the unmet critical needs of the expanding population in low, and middle-income countries. The situation is aggravated further by the significant impact of water bodies pollution, which raises the demands for fresh water. The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has reported that, by 2050, more than 5 billion people worldwide will have inadequate access to clean water. This problem can only be solved if new technologies are developed to transform polluted water from ubiquitous sources into potable and usable forms. To achieve this, low-cost and sustainable water purification systems for clean water supply must be implemented. This is particularly exigent in rural communities, where poverty is prevalent due to limited resources, and a lack of clean water complicates the already poor living conditions. 
In this project, we propose to develop multi-functional nanomaterials-based water purification systems composed of carbon nanoadsorbents (CNs) (capable of removing metal ions and organic pollutants from water), and porphyrins-nano-titanium dioxide (PT) (for visible-light powered photo-inactivation of pathogens in water). The proposed innovative technology is based on the fabrication of CNs and PT nano-formulations (CNPT) into compliant water filter membrane systems (CNPT-membranes) capable of all-in-one synergistic and simultaneous water treatment processes which include adsorption of pollutants, photoinactivation of microbes, viruses and anti-fouling. A practical application will be through the encasement of the CNPT-membranes in plastic components that can be incorporated into bespoke water treatment and storage containers. The prototype (containers) design will be based on translucent, and photosensitive plastic containers, so that with sunlight penetration, the water purifying CNPT-membrane systems will be more effective in destroying pathogens. In addition, a proprietary rapid and compostable paper-based biosensing technology will be developed to assess post-treatment water quality to inform and mitigating health risks. The concept of hippo water rollers will be integrated with the developed CNPT-membranes to make the system simple, efficient, and tailorable for both domestic and agricultural uses, particularly in rural settings. Thus, rolling of the containers after fetching from water sources would mechanically help to catalyse the simultaneous purification and photoinactivation processes, yielding self-sustaining smart water purification technology. A team of academic and industry experts will develop and implement the innovative water purification technology in the water-rich, but poorly served Democratic Republic of Congo as the beneficiary country, to help tackle poverty and address the UN Sustainable Development Goal on clean water and sanitation in the country."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Boosting the hydrogen economy in Brazil by developing Composite Palladium (Pd)/Graphene Oxide (GO) membranes for hydrogen purification.
descriptions:
"Hydrogen (H2) has been proposed as the most promising alternative to replace fossil fuels as an energy vector because of its high energy density and being water the only by-product from its combustion. This reaction takes place in Fuel Cells (FC), which transform the energy from the combustion of H2 into electricity, using H2 of high purity as fuel. Filling station networks for H2 cars are already available in some developed countries, but the application of FC in developing countries, such as Brazil, is not yet
a reality. Thus, it is imperative to establish policy frameworks that offer R&D assistance, aiding countries listed in the DAC to achieve their developmental goals within the H2 economy. However, currently, H2 is produced by steam methane reforming of gasification of coal involving the production of CO2/H2 mixtures. To obtain pure H2 to be used in FC, membrane separations play an important role as it has been proven already for gas separations. The aim of this project is to develop membranes to obtain purified H2 to be used in FC. Those membranes will be composite membranes formed by graphene oxide and palladium, which is an innovative development. Mathematical methods will be used to predict the performance and optimise membrane morphology. This progress will be carried out by joining research strategies that will be developed in Brazil and UK. The advancement of this technology in Brazil will elevate the country's position in adopting H2 as a clean and dependable fuel in accordance with relevant policies."

agency: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
titles: Defining degradative pathways and transport processes in 'plasticulture'
descriptions: Fellowship award investigating transport and fate of agricultural plastic and additives in soils, to determine whether potentially harmful compounds accumulate in the soil or are rendered harmless through assimilation by microbes. Focusses on the chemical release and impact of plastics on agriculture and water with research field studies in Egypt, India, Sri Lanka, Vietnam, and Kenya. SDG 15.
